title: Saul Becomes Paul
lead: The greatest opponent can become one of God’s most important instruments.
questions: Who is my Saul, the person I have stopped praying for, and to whom is God sending me today as an Ananias?
Can I talk about my own past the way Paul did: without whitewashing it, and with mercy as the punch line?
When someone we used to be afraid of walks into our church, what is my first word: “brother,” or “we’ll see”?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Yesterday we watched the church being born; today we meet the man who set out to wipe it out. Saul “was still breathing out murderous threats against the disciples of the Lord,” but he is no thug: he is the most gifted theologian of his generation, convinced he is defending God. He heads for Damascus with official letters authorizing him to arrest “men or women,” because from the very beginning women were no mere extras in this movement. The movement itself is called “the Way” here: not yet a doctrine, just a way of life. The most dangerous things in the history of religion have been done by devout people with Scripture on their lips. Zeal is no proof that you are right; sometimes it only measures your momentum.

Near Damascus a light stops him, and a question: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?” Me. After all, Saul had been persecuting people, but the risen Lord takes every blow aimed at His own as a blow aimed at Himself. Paul’s entire later theology of the church as the body of Christ was born in that one sentence, and it cuts both ways: whenever we wound any of His people, we touch the apple of His eye. Saul gets up blind; the official with the seals is led into the city by the hand. Three days of darkness, fasting, and the first prayer of his life not prayed as the top of the class. There are three days like that after which we see better than through years of perfect eyesight.

Then God sends not an apostle but an ordinary disciple. Ananias is honestly afraid: Lord, this man came here to arrest us. But he goes, lays his hands on the persecutor, and says, “Brother Saul.” The church’s first word to its tormentor was a family word. God accomplished the conversion on the road, but He needed a person to hold out a hand; without people like Ananias, no Damascus road has a sequel. And God accepted Saul in the middle of his error, not after he had reformed, and He did not break his temperament; He turned it around. The momentum of hatred became the momentum of mission.
This story forbids us to write people off. Pray for your Saul, the one who “will never change.” And when God turns him around, be an Ananias: let your first word be “brother,” not “we’ll see.”

Yesterday we watched the church being born. Today we meet the man who set out to wipe that church out. Luke introduces him without mincing words: Saul “was still breathing out murderous threats against the disciples of the Lord.” He is not a thug or a cynic. He is the most gifted young theologian of his generation, a student of the best school in Jerusalem, a man who would later write of his own past that as to zeal he persecuted the church, and as to righteousness in the law he was faultless. Saul did not destroy Jesus’ disciples against his conscience; he did it in keeping with it. He was dead certain he was defending God. And that is the first and most uncomfortable lesson of this story: the most dangerous things in the history of religion have been done by deeply devout people, with a sense of duty and Scripture on their lips. Zeal is no proof that you are right. Sometimes it only measures your momentum.

sections.heading: Letters in His Bag
paragraphs: It is worth seeing how official this persecution was. Saul goes to the high priest for letters to the synagogues in Damascus: documents authorizing arrests outside Judea and the transport of prisoners to Jerusalem. The warrant covers “men or women,” which lets slip, almost in passing, how important a role women played in the young church from the very beginning; nobody bothers arresting extras. The movement itself is called “the Way” in this text, and it is the oldest name for Christianity we know: not yet a doctrine, not an institution, just a way, a road you walk, a way of life. So Saul sets out with documents in his bag to block that Way. He has more than a hundred and thirty miles to walk and plenty of time to think. And at the end of that road waits not a victim but Someone who had been waiting for him in particular for a long time.

sections.heading: Why Do You Persecute Me?
paragraphs: Right outside Damascus a light from heaven flashes around him, and from the ground where he has fallen he hears a question: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?” Hidden in that question is a theology Saul was not ready for. He had not been persecuting Jesus, after all; Jesus was dead, or so Saul believed. He had been persecuting people: dragging men and women out of their homes, casting his vote for Stephen’s death. And the voice from heaven says “Me.” The risen Lord identifies with His people so literally that He takes a blow aimed at the least of them as a blow aimed at Himself. Saul asks the only sensible question left: “Who are You, Lord?” And he hears an answer that turns his world upside down: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.” Paul’s entire later theology of the church as the body of Christ was born in that one sentence, spoken to a persecutor lying in the dust. Whoever touches the community of believers touches Christ. That is worth remembering in the other direction too, inside the church: whenever we wound any of His people, even the least of them, even the one we think is most in the wrong, we touch the apple of His eye.

sections.heading: Three Days of Darkness
paragraphs: Saul gets up blind. The man who knew everything, who rode toward Damascus as an authority bearing official seals, is led into the city by the hand like a child. For three days he sees nothing, eats nothing, drinks nothing. This darkness is not a punishment; it is a place of transformation, a kind of tomb from which someone else will come out. Because in the middle of that darkness something happens that God notes with tenderness: “he is praying.” Every synagogue knew Saul’s prayers; he had been a man of prayer since childhood. But this is a different kind of prayer: the prayer of a man whose whole picture of the world has fallen apart, and who for the first time comes to God not as the top of the class. There are three days of darkness like that in life, after which we see better than through years of perfect eyesight.

sections.heading: Brother Saul
paragraphs: Then a hero steps onto the stage whom sermons rarely mention: Ananias, “a disciple” in Damascus. Not an apostle, not a prophet, just an ordinary believer in the city where an inquisitor with warrants was on his way. The Lord tells him to go to Straight Street and lay his hands on Saul of Tarsus. Ananias’s answer is wonderfully honest: Lord, many people have told me how much harm this man has done; he has come here to arrest us. Ananias doesn’t fake a courage he doesn’t have, and God doesn’t mock his fear; instead He shows him a piece of His plan: “Go!” And then: “This man is My chosen instrument to carry My name before the Gentiles and their kings.” And then comes a scene that is one of the most beautiful moments in the whole book of Acts. Ananias walks into the house, lays his hands on the man who came to put him in prison, and says, “Brother Saul.” Brother. The first word the church ever spoke to its persecutor was a family word. Not “prove yourself first,” not “we’ll see whether you can be trusted,” but: brother, the Lord Jesus has sent me so that you may see again. Something like scales falls from Saul’s eyes; he is baptized, eats, and regains his strength. God accomplished the conversion on the road, but He still needed a person to hold out a hand to the convert and call him brother. Without people like Ananias, no Damascus road has a sequel.

sections.heading: An Instrument with a Price
paragraphs: Notice what God says about Saul’s future: “This man is My chosen instrument,” and right after that: “I will show him how much he must suffer for My name.” The calling here is not a reward or a certificate of merit; it is a task with a price built in. The former persecutor will be persecuted from now on; the author of letters authorizing arrests will write letters from prison. The first installment of that price comes soon: right there in Damascus, the city he had come to as a hunter, he becomes the hunted and has to escape by night, lowered in a basket through an opening in the wall. The man who had ridden in on the main road with the high priest’s seals leaves the city in a cargo basket, like smuggled goods. And he never remembers that escape with shame; years later he describes it himself, because by then he had learned that God’s power likes to be perfected in weakness. And one more thing needs to be said plainly: God accepted Saul as he was, in the middle of his greatest mistake, not after he had reformed. He did not wait for Saul to do penance, think things over, and mellow. He stopped him at the full momentum of his hatred and turned that momentum into the momentum of mission. The same energy that drove him to Damascus with arrest warrants would later carry him across half the empire with the gospel. God doesn’t break people’s temperaments. He turns them around.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: This story is for three kinds of people. First, for those who have a Saul of their own: someone of whom people say, “That one will never change.” A militant opponent of faith in your family, someone who wounds the church or wounds you. This story forbids us to write people off. The greatest enemy the church ever had became its greatest missionary, and praying for today’s Sauls is one of the most biblical prayers we know. Second, for those who have their own road to Damascus behind them: a past they think makes it impossible to come to God. To the end of his life Paul remembered who he had been, and to the end of his life he kept saying that he had been shown mercy. Your past can become your strongest testimony, just as Paul’s past did. And third, for us as a community: the question is whether we know how to be Ananias. When a person with a history we used to fear walks into our church, is our first word “brother,” “sister,” or rather “we’ll see”? God took care of His part of the business with Saul out on the road. Our part is Straight Street: to go, lay on our hands, and call someone a brother whom yesterday we were afraid of. Everything hung on that one word: whether the converted Saul would become Paul, or remain a lonely, blind man in a stranger’s house.
